bullets: How one combined circuit works: inputs A, B and C feed an AND gate and a NOT gate, their outputs meet at an OR gate, and the truth table fills row by row
slides.heading: Logic gates: one circuit, alarm = (A AND B) OR (NOT C)
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one circuit gate by gate - and check what really switches the alarm on.

bullets: Describe the circuit alarm = (A AND B) OR (NOT C) and what each gate does
Work gate by gate through input combinations and fill in the truth table row by row
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to predict the alarm for any inputs.

bullets: Input A is switched on, so it feels as if the alarm must be on too
But A alone never reaches the alarm - so what else has to happen first?
slides.heading: A is on - is the alarm on?
slides.notes: Ask the class: A is on - is the alarm on? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because scene 3 tests exactly that case.

bullets: AND outputs 1 only when both its inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 when either input is 1; NOT flips its single input
The AND output and NOT C meet at the OR gate, and only the OR output drives the alarm
A truth table records the output for each combination of inputs
slides.heading: Read the circuit gate by gate
slides.notes: Stress the deciding habit: never jump from an input straight to the alarm - evaluate each gate in order, AND and NOT first, then OR.

bullets: Inputs A and B feed the AND gate; input C feeds the NOT gate
Both gate outputs meet at the OR gate, and the OR output drives the alarm
slides.heading: Meet the circuit: gates feed the alarm
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to each gate: follow the signal dot from A toward the AND gate and name every wire.

bullets: With A and B both 1, the AND output is 1
That 1 passes through the OR gate and switches the alarm on; the first truth table row fills in as 1 1 1 giving alarm 1
slides.heading: A and B on: the AND path lights the alarm
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and trace the signal: AND output to OR gate to alarm, then read the first truth table row aloud.

bullets: With B at 0 the AND output falls to 0, even though A is 1
With C at 1 the NOT output is also 0, so both OR inputs are 0 and the alarm stays off
slides.heading: B off and C on: the alarm stays off
slides.notes: Play scene 3 slowly: this is the row that breaks the guess that A alone is enough - both paths into the OR gate carry 0.

bullets: With C at 0, the NOT gate flips it to 1
That single 1 is enough for the OR gate, so the alarm switches on even though the AND output is 0
slides.heading: C off: NOT C alone lights the alarm
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and follow the NOT path: one 1 into the OR gate is enough, and the third truth table row fills in.

bullets: If A alone switched the alarm on, the row A=1, B=0, C=1 would give alarm 1
But in that row the AND output is 0 and NOT C is 0, so the OR output - and the alarm - is 0
slides.heading: Worked example: testing the A-alone claim in this circuit
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, state the A-alone claim. Step 2, evaluate the gates for A=1, B=0, C=1: AND gives 0, NOT gives 0. Step 3, OR of 0 and 0 is 0, so the alarm stays off - the claim fails, and only the gate-by-gate reading fits.

bullets: In pairs: for A=0, B=0, C=0, work out the AND output, NOT C and the alarm, gate by gate
Then swap and check: did you evaluate AND and NOT before OR?
slides.heading: Your turn: predict the next row
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for gate-by-gate working, then take two pairs answers.

bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who links the alarm straight to input A
Name both real routes to the alarm - A and B both on, or C off - to earn full credit
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers read the circuit gate by gate instead of jumping from one input to the alarm.
